purpose: Laronidase is used to treat a rare genetic condition called Mucopolysaccharidosis I (MPS I), also known as Hurler, Hurler-Scheie, or Scheie syndrome. Your body is missing or has very little of an important enzyme, and this medicine replaces it. It helps reduce the buildup of certain sugars in your body that can damage organs and tissues.
how_it_works: In MPS I, your body cannot break down certain complex sugars called glycosaminoglycans because it lacks a working enzyme called alpha-L-iduronidase. Laronidase is a man-made version of that missing enzyme given through an IV infusion. Once it enters your body, it gets into your cells and helps break down and clear out those harmful sugar buildups.
common_side_effects: Flushing (feeling warm or red in the face), rash or hives, headache, fever, chills, nausea, joint pain, swelling in the arms or legs, and reactions at the infusion site such as redness or discomfort. Infusion reactions during or shortly after the IV drip are fairly common.
warnings: Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis (a life-threatening reaction), can happen during or after the infusion. You will be watched closely during treatment and may be given antihistamines or other medicines before each infusion to reduce the risk. Tell your doctor right away if you have trouble breathing, chest tightness, swelling of the face or throat, or a rapid heartbeat. Let your care team know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 0.58 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given as an IV (intravenous) infusion once every week. The infusion is given slowly over several hours in a clinic or hospital setting so that healthcare providers can monitor you carefully throughout.
